posts.title: Quite for Cookies 0.22.7: the “trackers only” sweep could sign you out
body: The default sweep is called Trackers only, and until this version the popup told you it could not sign you out of anything, because nothing on its list of tracking domains was a site you could log in to.

That was not true. The list included analytics and marketing products, among them HubSpot, Mixpanel, Amplitude, Segment, Optimizely and New Relic, whose own customers sign in on those same addresses. The sweep matched the address rather than the cookie, so on those sites it removed everything, sign-in cookies included. If you use any of those tools for work, a sweep may have signed you out of them.

The safety promise was written in a comment rather than enforced in the code. It is now enforced. Anything that looks like a sign-in is spared in both sweeps, and the checkbox that controls it works in both. It used to be greyed out in the default sweep, so it could not even be switched on.

Three other ways data could go that should not have are fixed in the same release. Closing a tab in an Incognito window could clear the ordinary profile's cookies and stored data for that site. Unticking a row did not always protect it, when two cookies shared an address. And a site with no cookies could never be added to the spared list, while the automatic clear would still wipe its stored data.
Nothing about this was reported by a user. It came out of an audit we ran on our own published code before adding a fourth extension.

posts.title: Quite for Facebook is on the Chrome Web Store
body: Quite for Facebook hides the clutter from your feed and does nothing else: posts marked Sponsored or Ad, suggested posts from pages you do not follow, suggested groups, and the Sponsored column on the right.

Two options are worth knowing about. Strict mode only hides posts that are also marked “Suggested for you”, for anyone who wants it to err on the cautious side. A placeholder option leaves a small strip with a Show button where a post was, so you can always see what was hidden and put it back, which is also the honest way to check it is not hiding things you wanted.
It runs only on facebook.com. It has no account and no server, and nothing is sent to us.
It is free, MIT licensed, and the source is on GitHub.

posts.title: Quite for YouTube: saying what it actually does
body: The store listing says Quite for YouTube stops most video ads loading. We spent a day trying to measure that and could not show it was true, so we have taken the claim out. The corrected listing is with the Chrome Web Store now and replaces the current one once it is approved.

What it does, and what we can demonstrate: it skips video ads as they appear, fast-forwards the ones that cannot be skipped, and hides the ad panels in the feed, sidebar, search results and Shorts. The listing will say that instead. This site already does.

The same update removes a counter from the extension's popup. It reported videos protected, and on inspection it was counting videos that had no advert to begin with. A number that flatters is worse than no number, so it is gone. The two that remain, ads skipped and time saved, are both counted from adverts actually seen.
The setting that does the stripping stays, renamed to Strip ad schedule, and stays on by default. It does no harm. We simply cannot show you what it prevents, so we no longer say.

posts.title: Quite for Cookies is on the Chrome Web Store
body: Quite for Cookies shows you what a site has stored before it deletes anything, lets you pick what goes, and then re-reads the site to prove it actually went. It can also clear a site automatically when you close its last tab.
Sign-in cookies are left alone unless you say otherwise, so clearing a site does not sign you out of it.
It is free, MIT licensed, and the source is on GitHub.

posts.title: Some videos start black and silent instead of playing
body: On some videos an advert still gets through. When it does, the player can sit black and silent instead of playing either the advert or your video. It looks like the extension has broken, which is the worst way for this to fail, so it is worth saying plainly what is happening.

The extension does not block requests. It stops YouTube issuing an ad schedule in the first place, which is what keeps your session out of the anti-adblock net. It does not catch every response, and on the ones it misses an advert starts inside a player that was not expecting one.

There is deliberately no automatic recovery. An earlier version reloaded the player after a stall; measured over repeated loads it produced a YouTube error screen more often than it rescued anything, so it was taken out. A stuck video you can reload is better than an error screen you cannot.

Reload the video and it usually plays. If it sticks again, add ?ytacoff=1 to the end of the URL. That loads that one video with the extension switched off, which is also how to confirm the extension is what is causing it rather than YouTube having a bad day.
This is why we do not claim to stop every advert. Saying otherwise would earn one-star reviews describing exactly this.
works: Feed, sidebar, search and Shorts ad panels are still hidden
Overlay banners drawn on top of the video are still removed
Most video ads are still stopped before they load, and skippable ones still get skipped
Nothing about your account, watch history or any other tab is touched

posts.title: The YouTube counter was measuring the same thing twice
body: The popup showed two all-time figures, “Ads stopped” and “Ads skipped”. They were always the same number, because the code incremented both on consecutive lines. One of them was never a measurement of anything.

Version 0.31.0 separates them. “Ads skipped” still counts what it always counted: an ad that reached the player and was skipped or fast-forwarded. The other now counts something genuinely different: videos where the ad schedule was stopped before the player ever saw it. That one is labelled “Videos protected”, which is what it counts.

It credits once per video rather than once per stopped response, because a single video can produce several: a retry, or returning to the same watch page. Counting each would inflate the figure with work done twice on one video.

Stored totals are reset once on upgrade. Every previous value was a copy of the skip count, and carrying it forward would have left a number that was never true sitting under a label that now means something specific. The counter starts again from zero, honestly.

Update, later the same day: the counter this post describes has been removed from the extension. Separating it from the skip count was right, but once it stood on its own it turned out to be counting videos that never had an advert in the first place, which made it flattering rather than useful. The popup now shows two figures, ads skipped and time saved, both counted from adverts actually seen.

posts.title: Quite for Cookies
body: A third extension. It shows exactly what a site has stored in your browser. Every cookie, grouped by the domain that set it, with sizes, and the ones holding your sign-in marked as such. It removes only what you pick.

Then it counts again and tells you what actually went: how many were removed, how many could not be, and how many the page has already set again because it is still open. Those numbers come from re-reading the browser rather than assuming the delete worked.

Version 0.20.0 adds a sweep that runs on its own. Turn on “clear a site when I close its last tab” and the job happens in the background as you browse, sparing sign-ins and anything on your spared list. Chrome's own session-only setting cannot do this. It waits until you close the entire browser. Every sweep is recorded, so a run that cleared nothing can never be mistaken for one that worked.
It installs with no access to any website. Access is asked for one domain at a time, at the moment you press the button, and is reversible from the popup.
